detail.title: Tides of Subordination: Fiscal Constraint, Financialised Commodity Cycles, and the Political Economy of Latin America
detail.abstract: This paper explores how Latin American progressive governments are constrained in using fiscal policy for redistribution, stabilization, and structural transformation due to two key forces: structural dependence on commodity exports and the financialization of global commodity markets. While Keynesian theory emphasizes public investment as central to equitable development, Latin American states face shrinking fiscal space due to volatile global markets driven by speculative capital. These forces decouple commodity prices from productive fundamentals, exposing governments to boom-bust cycles beyond their control. Even with democratic mandates for change, fiscal sovereignty is undermined, pushing states toward austerity when expansion is most needed. Through comparative analysis, the paper shows how financial speculation shapes domestic politics, often curtailing progressive ambitions. It calls for rethinking global economic governance to restore democratic control over fiscal policy and support an economy centred on equity, sustainability, and autonomy, echoing Keynes's critique of austerity and his call for active government intervention.

title: Examining the Predictors of Unit Price of a Readymade Garment in Bangladesh
affiliations: Canadian University of Bangladesh and Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP)

detail.title: Examining the Predictors of Unit Price of a Readymade Garment in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Purpose-The prime objective of the present research study was to determine the antecedents of unit price for a readymade garment 'XYZ' and to investigate the influence of three variable-raw material, quality labor cost, quality cost on per unit price. Design/methodology/approach-In this study a simple random sample has been drawn constituting production manager as the sample unit. The present study used a sample of 50 RMG companies. Further, the influences of predictor variables on the per unit price has been assessed using multiple linear regression analysis. Findings-The findings in this paper supports the two variables; raw material and quality because result revealed that both are significant whereas, labor cost is insignificant. It implies that labour cost is not influencing the unit price. Research limitations/implications-The paper leads to a research question for future researcherswhy labor cost is non-significant predictor of unit price? despite being very much important theoretically. Limitations of the paper include the data that is specific to Bangladesh RMG industry, therefore it cannot be generalised, further the economic meltdown due to COVID-19 pandemic might have influenced the results. Originality/value-The paper's prime contribution is based on the assessment of predictor variables and their influence on unit price of readymade garment XYZ. It is based on the estimates provided by the production manager.

title: Marketing, Market Power, and Welfare
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Marketing, Market Power, and Welfare
detail.abstract: Since the mid-1990s, the United States has experienced a joint rise in aggregate marketing intensity and in the correlation between firms' marketing-to-production cost ratios (MPCR) and markups. I develop a dynamic general equilibrium model with heterogeneous firms and endogenous markups in which marketing serves as a signal of unobserved product quality. The model shows that more scalable marketing technologies-such as those enabled by the Internet-intensify signaling competition, raising both the MPCR-markup correlation and aggregate marketing intensity. Calibrated to U.S. data, a 40% increase in the scalability of marketing technology accounts for these patterns but generates welfare losses of about 1.7% of steady-state consumption. Comparing the market equilibrium with the constrained-efficient allocation, I show that information frictions and variable markups jointly depress entry and productivity. Targeted policies-such as size-dependent subsidies and entry support-can mitigate these distortions and deliver substantial welfare gains.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12237
title: Industrialization and the Return to Labor: Evidence from Prussia
affiliations: University of Cologne - Center for Macroeconomic Research (CMR) and University of Cologne - Center for Macroeconomic Research (CMR)

detail.title: Industrialization and the Return to Labor: Evidence from Prussia

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Industrialization boosts aggregate incomes, but its distributional effects remain debated. We study the impact of coal-driven industrialization on unskilled labor incomes using novel panel data on wages from 667 Prussian localities (1800-1879), extended with county-level data through 1914. Exploiting spatial variation in coal proximity in difference-in-differences and event-study designs, we find that wage gains in coal-rich regions emerged once industrialization accelerated in the 1850s and continued to grow until WWI. Evidence from 3,000 household accounts shows that coal proximity raised labor incomes primarily for low-skilled workers, with weaker effects for high-skilled and mechanical occupations. This pattern suggests that industrialization reduced wage inequality by compressing the local skill premium. Mediation analysis indicates that wage gains for unskilled workers were primarily driven by technology adoption and the increasing demand for low-skilled labor, rather than by sectoral change or the spread of the factory system.

title: How Does Big Data Development Affect Urban Environmental Welfare Performance in China? Evidence from National Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zones
affiliations: Fuyang Normal University, Fuyang Normal University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Does Big Data Development Affect Urban Environmental Welfare Performance in China? Evidence from National Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zones

keywords: Staggered DID model with heterogeneous effects

detail.abstract: Accurately assessing the impact of big data pilot zone policies on urban environmental welfare performance is of considerable importance for resolving the tensions among economic, environmental, and social dimensions; for advancing a green and inclusive development paradigm; and for realizing modernization characterized by harmonious coexistence between humans and nature. Treating national-level comprehensive big data pilot zones as a quasi-natural experiment, this study measures urban environmental welfare performance using an EBM-Network-DEA approach based on a panel of 282 Chinese prefecture-level and higher cities from 2003 to 2023, and estimates a staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) model that accommodates heterogeneous dynamic effects to identify the causal impact of the pilot zones. The empirical results show that the big data pilot zone policy significantly improves urban environmental welfare performance, and this finding is robust to a range of checks including endogeneity tests, placebo simulations, and machine-learning based estimations. Mechanism analysis indicates that the policy promotes overall improvements in environmental welfare performance through multiple channels summarized as “technical efficiency gains — pollution reduction — social welfare enhancement.” Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the policy effect is stronger in central and western cities, cities with lower administrative ranks, non-old industrial base cities, and non-resource-dependent cities. Moreover, the policy generates significant spatial spillover effects: within a 100-kilometer radius around pilot cities, neighboring non-pilot cities experience measurable gains. These findings provide policy implications for leveraging big data to sustain China’s path to modernization.

title: Financial Deepening and Input–Output Linkages: Thresholds and Shocks in Latin America and Emerging Asia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial Deepening and Input–Output Linkages: Thresholds and Shocks in Latin America and Emerging Asia
detail.abstract: This study examines how financial deepening (FD) relates to structural change in emerging economies, conditional on shock regimes and the density of input–output linkages (2020–2022). Fixed-effects panel models (country–year and country–sector) incorporate interactions by regime (COVID-19, 2022 geopolitical shock) and by network index (Z_ROTOT01). The dependent variables are: (i) the combined share of manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services (KIS), and (ii) sectoral share variation, controlling for demand composition. At the country–year level, FD is negative for KIS+manufacturing, but the interaction FD×post_war22 is positive and significant, evidencing a regime shift in 2022. Diversification (1–HHI) declines markedly that year. In Latin America, FD turns positive beyond a network threshold. Public and external demand display stabilising effects. FD’s effectiveness is regime- and network-dependent: without dense linkages, credit locks structure; with them, it enables upgrading. Policy implications stress link densification, targeted finance, and functional diversity.

title: Crisis Shock, ESG Investment and Stock Performance
affiliations: Guangzhou College of Commerce and Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics

detail.title: Crisis Shock, ESG Investment and Stock Performance
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investment in mitigating the shock of crises on stock performance. We develop an asset pricing model in which investors’ decisions incorporate both ESG factors and exogenous crisis shocks. Our theoretical model indicates that ESG investment mitigates the negative effect of crises on stock performance, particularly for highly affected stocks. We empirically test this prediction using the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment, analyzing Chinese A-share listed firms from October 2019 to May 2020. The results show that a higher ESG level significantly improves the excess returns of stocks highly impacted by the crisis but has no statistically significant effect on those with low impact. These findings are consistent with our theoretical predictions. We find that ESG investing mitigates negative shocks by adjusting stocks’ market betas—an important channel for its impact on asset returns. This research contributes to understanding the differential impact of ESG investment on stock performance during crises and underscores financial capital’s role in promoting corporate green transformation.

title: Innovation, Financial Deepening, and Income Inequality in Six G7 Economies: A Break-Robust Causality Analysis (1980–2023)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Innovation, Financial Deepening, and Income Inequality in Six G7 Economies: A Break-Robust Causality Analysis (1980–2023)
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the links between income inequality and two macro drivers—innovation and financial deepening—in six G7 economies (France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States) over 1980–2023. We estimate country-specific Fourier Toda–Yamamoto (FTY) vector autoregressions that accommodate mixed integration orders and unknown smooth structural breaks. Two key results emerge. First, R&D intensity and the Gini index form a bidirectional loop in five countries; in Italy inequality-to-R&D dominance is evident. Second, financial deepening Granger-causes inequality in all cases, consistent with the dynamic Financial Kuznets Curve, while inequality-to-finance feedback in the United States, France and Italy highlights the social endogeneity of finance. Robustness checks—alternative lags, Fourier frequencies, and sub-samples around the Global Financial Crisis and the pandemic—leave directions unchanged. Policy implications are cluster-specific, emphasising inclusive-finance guardrails, redistribution-first strategies, and fintech outreach.

title: State-Contingent Cross-Asset Connectedness in Crisis: TVP-VAR Evidence from U.S. Equities, Crypto, and Commodities
affiliations: Institute of Business Management (IoBM), IQRA University, University of Regensburg - Institute of Business Management, affiliation not provided to SSRN, SZABIST, Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka and Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka

detail.title: State-Contingent Cross-Asset Connectedness in Crisis: TVP-VAR Evidence from U.S. Equities, Crypto, and Commodities
detail.abstract: This study examines crisis-era risk transmission across U.S. equities, US Dollar Index, major cryptocurrencies, and benchmark commodities employing actual market data spanning from April 4, 2016, to September 30, 2025. A time-varying parameter vector autoregressive model (TVP-VAR) was used with stochastic volatility and generalized forecast-error variance decompositions. The main objective of this research is to examine three major crises: COVID-19, the Russia-Ukraine war, and the Israel-Palestine conflict. Examination of these timeframes reveals that the role different asset classes change notably when uncertainty is high. The results show that system-wide connectedness increases significantly in the time of crises. with external spillovers serving as a main contributor in the initial phases of each event. U.S. equities seem to remain consistent transmitters of risk, with Ethereum (ETH) assuming a growing role as a transmitter, exceeding Bitcoin (BTC). Commodities, including crude oil and precious metals, exhibit dynamic roles based on the phase of the crisis, sometimes acting as receivers and as transmitters in other instances. This research extends existing literature by offering a frequency-aware, multi-asset model of financial contagion, emphasizing the dynamic behavior of asset classes in times of crises and their implications for portfolio management strategies.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12236
title: How New Business Models Shape Innovation Spillovers: Insights from the New Space Economy
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology and Dresden University of Technology

detail.title: How New Business Models Shape Innovation Spillovers: Insights from the New Space Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Those seeking to drum up public support for the space industry frequently cite its potential to generate valuable spillovers to other industries. However, existing research on spillover effects overlooks differences in business models among commercial actors and focuses only on individual projects or specific space agencies. We analyze how evolving business models influence spillovers by comparing the dynamic capabilities of traditional aerospace conglomerates to those of new space firms, using a unique dataset of 35,696 space-related patent applications. We find that, in addition to industries directly related to space, such as aeronautics, sectors like manufacturing and communication technology in particular benefit from space activities. At the firm level, we observe that new space business models present greater spillover potential and generate more spillovers than traditional aerospace conglomerates. However, traditional conglomerates such as Airbus or Boeing induce spillovers into digital systems and clean tech, while new space firms cannot translate their digital business models into digital spillovers and occupy more peripheral positions in the innovation network of space. Additionally, based on two different innovation metrics and more than 1.6 million additional patent applications, we find no evidence that the business models of the space industry have generally led to more spillovers than other high-tech industries.

title: ESG and Bank Loan Cost
affiliations: National Yunlin University of Science and Technology - Department of Finance and National Yunlin University of Science and Technology

detail.title: ESG and Bank Loan Cost
detail.abstract: This study examines how Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance influences bank lending conditions in Taiwan's capital markets, analysing 2,918 firm-year observations from 2016 to 2023. Employing instrumental variables estimation to address simultaneity between interest rates and collateral requirements, we find that superior ESG performance significantly reduces both tangible borrowing costs (interest rates) and intangible costs (collateral requirements). A one-standard-deviation increase in ESG scores corresponds to approximately 6.7 basis point interest rate reductions and 3.2 percentage point decreases in collateral probability. Dimensional decomposition reveals differential effects across ESG pillars, with social responsibility demonstrating strongest influence on interest rates whilst environmental performance proves most effective for collateral relief. Exploiting the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock through difference-in-differences methodology, we provide causal evidence that ESG performance functions as crisis-resilience insurance. High-ESG firms secured additional 10-11 basis point interest rate advantages and 9-27 percentage point collateral requirement reductions during the pandemic compared to low-ESG peers. Our findings advance sustainable finance literature by providing the first comprehensive analysis of ESG effects across multiple lending dimensions simultaneously in an Asian emerging market context, demonstrating that sustainability practices generate quantifiable financial benefits through reduced financing frictions whilst offering enhanced protection during periods of market stress.

title: Labor Mobility, Innovation Risk, and the Valuation of Immigration Policy
affiliations: Northwestern University, Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: Immigration, Growth, and the Asset-Price Nexus
detail.abstract: I build a continuous-time macro-finance model to study how U.S. immigration policy shapes innovation, long-run growth, asset prices, and welfare. Immigration affects the economy through two margins: the composition of inflows (skilled versus unskilled) and their scale. Skilled immigration expands research capacity and accelerates technological progress, while low-skill inflows reduce manual wages and weaken incentives to automate. These forces generate a sharp growth–asset price nexus: policies that raise expected growth also increase long-horizon uncertainty and risk premia, whereas restrictive policies reduce both. Welfare analysis shows that temporary immigration shocks have modest effects, but permanent reforms have large and lasting consequences because they shift the economy’s long-run growth path. Skilled-immigration tightening is strongly welfare-reducing, enforcement of undocumented labor delivers only small welfare gains, and liberal immigration reform—combining higher skilled admissions with legalization of low-skill labor—produces substantial welfare improvements. Immigration policy is therefore a central determinant of U.S. long-run macroeconomic and financial stability.

title: The Externality of Foreign Investor Disclosure
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE), University of Toronto, Rotman School of Management, University of International Business and Economics and City University of New York, Baruch College - Zicklin School of Business - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: The Externality of Foreign Investor Disclosure
detail.abstract: We examine the influence of foreign equity flows on China's unique retail-dominated stock market, identifying a novel channel through which investors' herding creates significant market externalities. We find that the daily disclosure of foreign investors' positions induces local investors to imitate these trades, resulting in observable short-term price distortions followed by reversals. Our analyses, which include inflow predictability tied to disclosure timing and path analysis decomposition, confirm that the herding effect, largely driven by retail participants, is more impactful than the direct effect based on the informational content of foreign capital. Furthermore, inflated stock prices resulting from the herding behavior cause public firms to overvalue and overinvest, leading to reduced investment efficiencies. These findings highlight potential adverse consequences stemming from specific market liberalization designs.

title: Global Geopolitical Disaster Risk and Bond Risk Premia
affiliations: Xiamen University, Central University of Finance and Economics, Central University of Finance and Economics and Xiamen University

detail.title: Global Geopolitical Disaster Risk and Bond Risk Premia
detail.abstract: Using geopolitical risk indices for 44 countries and regions, we construct a global geopolitical disaster risk (GPDR) measure defined as the crosscountry skewness of idiosyncratic geopolitical risk. Empirically, GPDR significantly forecasts the U.S. Treasury bond risk premia in-and out-of-sample and delivers sizable economic value. Its predictive power is not spanned by the yield curve, macroeconomic predictors, and level-based geopolitical risk measures. An affine term structure model shows that GPDR's incremental predictive power operates through the market price of level risk, reinforcing the countercyclical term premium. High GPDR also forecasts weaker subsequent real activity and predicts interest rate expectation errors, credit spreads, and Treasury auction outcomes.

title: Dollar Erosion: Understanding the Loss of Reserve Currency Status
affiliations: , Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University and New York University (NYU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Dollar Erosion: Understanding the Loss of Reserve Currency Status
detail.abstract: The U.S. dollar depreciated in April 2025 while domestic interest rates rose relative to Euro, the VIX increased, and the convenience yield on 1-year Treasurys fell relative to foreign-currency safe assets. These patterns represent a marked departure from historical correlations. Notably, the decline in the dollar convenience yield predates the April 2025 shock by two years. Our theoretical analysis shows that these movements are consistent with shifts in global demand for U.S. dollar safe assets and the perception that the U.S. may lose its reserve currency status. Using a calibrated model, we find that the loss of demand for dollar safe assets leads to a steady-state depreciation of the dollar of around 7.6%, decline in U.S. dollar safe asset convenience yield of 0.9%, and an increase in U.S. long-term interest rates of 0.9%.

title: Whither Central Clearing Counterparties? Counterparty Risk In Stablecoin-Based Securities Settlement
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Whither Central Clearing Counterparties? Counterparty Risk In Stablecoin-Based Securities Settlement
detail.abstract: Recent research suggests that distributed ledger technologies (DLTs) could mitigate counterparty credit risk in post-trade processes by enabling atomic settlement and potentially reducing reliance on central clearing counterparties (CCPs), thereby lowering both clearing and settlement costs. This article offers a critical perspective on that proposition. While DLT-based securities settlement can ensure accuracy for assets already recorded on chain, participants remain exposed to the redemption counterparty risk-stablecoins and other digital tokens may not be adequately backed by real-world assets. The article examines a range of policy responses to these challenges. First, natively digital settlement assets-such as central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) or tokenized equity issued directly by corporations-address redemption counterparty risk because they exist entirely within the DLT system. In addition, legally mandated redemption rights, the assignment of super-priority status to claims, and the placement of reserves in bankruptcy-remote entities can strengthen the enforceability of redemption rights. Finally, the article argues for the potential of a short-term, mutualized insurance mechanism to protect token holders' redemption claims.

title: Simply Can't Wait: Evaluating the Effect of California's Fast-Food Minimum Wage Increase
affiliations: Northeastern University (USA)

detail.title: Simply Can't Wait: Evaluating the Effect of California's Fast-Food Minimum Wage Increase
detail.abstract: This paper estimates short-run employment effects of California's sectoral minimum wage for fast-food restaurants. On April 1, 2024, covered limited-service chains faced a $20 hourly floor while the statewide minimum wage was $16 (up from $15.50 in 2023). Using establishment-level mobility data and a difference-indifferences design restricted to "clean" counties without local wage ordinances, I proxy on-site staffing with weekly long-duration device visits (¿4 hours). Baseline estimates indicate an average 8% decline in on-site employment at treated outlets relative to comparable full-service and retail establishments. An event-study shows no pre-trends and a gradual, persistent post-announcement decline, consistent with anticipatory staffing adjustments. Placebo estimates for exempt "enclosed" venues are null, and effects are similar across urban and rural locations. The results imply that a sectoral wage floor induces meaningful reductions in labor utilization on intensive margins (hours, shift density) rather than immediate large-scale job loss.

reference: Journal of Accounting Research, Forthcoming
title: A Tale of Two Banks: When Credit Loss Models Meet Economic Crises
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Accounting and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (AMSS)

detail.title: A Tale of Two Banks: When Credit Loss Models Meet Economic Crises
detail.abstract: Policymakers and researchers are concerned that the expected credit loss (ECL) approach may exacerbate procyclicality. Using administrative loan-level and firm-level data in China, we find that banks adopting the ECL model reduced their credit supply and became more prudent in lending decisions after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, compared to banks using the incurred credit loss (ICL) approach. Our findings are more pronounced for banks that experienced greater loan loss provisions induced by ECL and for firms with higher credit risk. The credit contraction persisted throughout our sample period. We further document that firms more exposed to ECL banks experienced larger reductions in loans, assets, liabilities, and revenue after the pandemic began than those more exposed to ICL banks. These findings support the conjecture that the ECL approach may exacerbate procyclicality.

title: The Theory of Vertex Synthesis: A Universal Framework for Predicting Breakthroughs in Complex System

detail.title: The Theory of Vertex Synthesis: A Universal Framework for Predicting Breakthroughs in Complex System
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Theory of Vertex Synthesis (TVS), a novel formal framework for analyzing and predicting qualitative leaps—or breakthroughs—in complex systems. TVS posits that such breakthroughs become possible if and only if the Entropy of Fragments (H(K)) within a system exceeds the Entropy of Control (H(Δ)). We formalize this core law mathematically and demonstrate its explanatory power through three heterogeneous case studies: the physical water-ice phase transition, the collapse of Eastman Kodak due to digital disruption, and the dissolution of the USSR. TVS provides a unified language for phenomena previously described disparately as revolutions, phase transitions, or innovations, offering a meta-theoretical lens for interdisciplinary research.

reference: 74 STAN. L. REV. ONLINE 67 (2022)
title: Ascertaining the President-Elect Under the Presidential Transition Act
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Law

detail.title: Ascertaining the President-Elect Under the Presidential Transition Act
detail.abstract:
The Presidential Transition Act (PTA) requires the Administrator of the General Services Administration (GSA) to facilitate the transition to an incoming administration following a presidential election. The GSA must provide a President-elect with office space, telecommunications services, and millions of dollars for transition staff, consultants, and travel. Other agencies must conduct background checks on a President-elect's intended nominees for national security positions as expeditiously as possible.

The PTA does not provide any guidance for the GSA Administrator, however, in determining whether a presidential candidate qualifies as a President-elect. The statute defines the term “President-elect” as “the apparent successful candidate[] for the office of President . . . as ascertained by the Administrator.” But the statute provides no standards for an Administrator to apply in ascertaining an election’s results or determining whether a candidate is apparently successful. In most years, the Administrator’s decision is straightforward because the losing major-party candidate concedes on, or shortly after, election night. The presidential elections of 2000 and 2020, in contrast, involved lengthy post-election controversies. In both cases, the Administrator delayed ascertaining a President-elect for several weeks. Disputes arose over the standards the Administrator was employing in ascertaining—or declining to ascertain—the election’s apparent results, and whether the Administrator was improperly motivated by partisan considerations. 

This Article provides a framework for Administrators to apply, and Congress to consider codifying, when ascertaining the results of presidential elections under the PTA. It further suggests that Congress should amend the PTA to avoid unnecessarily delays in presidential transitions by requiring the GSA and other agencies to provide the full extent of transition-related services to all major presidential candidates if an election’s results cannot be ascertained within three days of Election Day. Finally, since the Administrator lacks constitutional authority to definitively determine a presidential election’s result, Congress should reduce the potential perceived significance of the Administrator’s ascertainment decision by changing the term “President-elect” as used in the PTA and related federal statutes to a less politically charged term, such as “federal designee.”

title: An Index-Based Approach to Formalizing John Rawls's Theory of Justice
affiliations: Zaporizhzhya Aviation Vocational College named after O. H. Ivchenko

detail.title: An Index-Based Approach to Formalizing John Rawls's Theory of Justice
detail.abstract: This paper presents an attempt to formalize Rawls's theory of justice. The formalization is based on the three core principles of Rawls's theory: the Greatest Equal Liberty Principle, the Fair Equality of Opportunity Principle, and the Difference Principle. For each principle, a corresponding quantitative index is proposed: the Basic Liberties Index (BLI), the Equality of Opportunity Index (EOI), and the Least Advantaged Welfare Index (LAWI). These indices are constructed using established global metrics such as the World Press Freedom Index, the Democracy Index, the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index, and the Palma Ratio. Finally, a composite Rawls's Index of Justice (RIJ) is proposed as an average of these three indices to provide a holistic measure of a society's alignment with Rawlsian principles.

title: The Role of Social Science Research Network (SSRN) on Uprising Researchers: The Case Study of Thee Benjamin Masama
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants, Mirracle Consultants and Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: The Role of Social Science Research Network (SSRN) on Uprising Researchers: The Case Study of Thee Benjamin Masama
detail.abstract: Research is critical in the development of societies around the world. Apart from raising awareness about trending phenomenon, research also brings to light areas for future studies. However, in the academic field many promising researchers are thwarted at early stages, due to harsh reviews from journal reviewers. However, there are platforms like the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), that offers a platform to uprising researchers without exposing them to discouraging reviews. This was the case for Benjamin Masama, a researcher who became a force to be reckoned with in specific research areas like Blockchain Technology (BT). Thus, the main objective of this study was to interrogate how SSRN contribute to the growth of uprising researchers. To achieve the above, desktop literature review was predominantly used to summarise all the publications of Benjamin Masama on SSRN. In addition, an interview was conducted to gain more insights into the publications. From the results obtained, it was evident that Benjamin Masama is mostly interested in African economic development, blockchain technology, entrepreneurship, risk management, intelligence, governance, and spirituality; thereby making him a versatile researcher. It was further ascertained that he has a book published under his name, and two articles published in an international journal. From the above, it was concluded that SSRN plays two major roles which are; 1) to boost researcher confidence and 2) exposes uprising researchers to a wider audience. Consequently, it was recommended that SSRN be used as a tool in grooming research skills at the undergraduate level.

title: Regulating AI-Generated Inventions: Should Patent Laws Be Amended to Accommodate AI Creativity? LLM Dissertation Course: Information Technology and Intellectual Property Law

detail.title: Regulating AI-Generated Inventions: Should Patent Laws Be Amended to Accommodate AI Creativity? LLM Dissertation Course: Information Technology and Intellectual Property Law

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or personal data and therefore did not require ethical approval.

detail.abstract: he system of patent law remains structurally founded on a fundamental assumption that only a natural person can invent. This person-centric doctrine is responsible for the possession and enforcement of patent rights. With artificial intelligence systems like DABUS producing more outputs that pass the statutory of patentability criteria, this presumption has come under significant doctrinal and normative pressure. Under the existing UK and EU regulations, the invention of legal personhood, mental conception, and the capacity to confer rights are also prerequisites to being an inventor, which in turn excludes autonomous AI systems in turn. This has been reaffirmed in judicial decisions in Thaler v Comptroller-General and EPO rulings J 8/20 and J 9/20. However, as revealed via a comparative study of DABUS litigation in Germany, South Africa, the United States, Australia, and China, a doctrinaire approach can be harmful to the innovation incentives, legal certainty, and legitimacy of the patent system. The analysis does not favor statutory reform or personhood of AI, but instead argues the application of a doctrine-preserving approach based on legal consistency and institutional practicality. The study suggests an attribution test to determine the human actual deviser in AI assisted invention, anti-data dumping adequacy criteria, provenance artefacts as evidence of conception, and administrative elucidation by way of UKIPO and EPO practice notices. WIPO as a source of soft-law convergence is also suggested to overcome global divergence without sacrificing domestic doctrinal consistency. The dissertation argues that a human-centred framework can be adopted and symbolic attribution to nonpersons should be rejected, so that legal integrity can be preserved without shutting out AI-enabled innovation. This study propose doctrine preserving reforms that safeguard human-centred inventorship while accommodating AI- enabled innovation.

title: A Proposal for a Permanent Multilateral Investment Court as a Substitute for the Existing ISDS Regime

detail.title: A Proposal for a Permanent Multilateral Investment Court as a Substitute for the Existing ISDS Regime
detail.abstract: Despite being in existence and functioning since the 1960s, the current Investor-State Dispute Settlement system is subjected to significant criticism for its perceived failures including but not limited to arbitrator bias, inconsistent awards across jurisdictions and the consequent lack of predictability as well as the incurrence of extraordinary costs. Employing the doctrinal research methodology, the author has proposed a one-stop solution, i.e., the establishment of a Multilateral Investment Court to overcome the aforementioned challenges. This would essentially entail having a two-tiered mechanism comprising a first instance tribunal and an appellate tribunal with specialized, full-time arbitrators. The paper examines specific procedural improvements including transparent arbitrator appointment processes, specialized expertise requirements, and cost reduction measures. It further explores the potential of the establishment of an Advisory Centre which would provide research support and enhance the efficiency of the system. By virtue of this paper, the author seeks to critically examine the effectiveness and functioning of existing treaty-based ISDS regime and proposes the establishment of a Permanent Multilateral Investment Court as a viable alternative to the same. The findings suggest that the proposed structure could significantly improve uniformity in practice and arbitral awards while reducing forum shopping. This research also aims to contribute to the ongoing UNCITRAL Working Group III deliberations on ISDS reform by offering a comprehensive framework.

title: Nigeria's Climate Action Strategy: How Regulations can be used by Nigeria in Furtherance of its Climate and Sustainability Governance

detail.title: Nigeria's Climate Action Strategy: How Regulations can be used by Nigeria in Furtherance of its Climate and Sustainability Governance
detail.abstract: Countries in the world are working hand in glove against a mutual enemy known as climate change which has been ravaging communities and which virulent scourge is being felt excruciatingly by certain territories designated to be more vulnerable to it. Nigeria like many nations in the world has taken a brittle defence against this menacing enemy. Climate scientists have recommended numerous measures with which we can backpedal the apocalypse already caused and obviate the apocalyptic forecast predicted to be caused by climate change. This paper burrows deep into how Nigeria can utilize regulations to contribute its quota to the fight against climate change.

title: Concealed-Carry Permits and Firearm Sales Are Low-Dimensional
affiliations: University of Central Missouri - Economics & Finance and Williams College

detail.title: Concealed-Carry Permits and Firearm Sales Are Low-Dimensional

detail.abstract: We use principal component analysis to examine population-adjusted, county-level counts of concealed-carry permits across 1,111 counties in 15 states (2006-2019) and gun sales across 168 counties in 4 states (2008-2020). Both measures are low-dimensional, indicating that most county-level variation can be summarized by a small number of stable common factors. The results reveal that gun sales and concealed-carry permitting are spatially patterned and highly persistent over time. This pattern suggests that long-run local characteristics-such as culture, institutions, and state regulatory environments-shape permitting levels, whereas short-term, within-county changes (for example, annual fluctuations in crime) contribute relatively little to observed variation. Because firearm prevalence is a recognized determinant of injury, mortality, and public health expenditure, understanding its structural stability is essential for healtheconomic evaluation and for designing effective interventions. By documenting the structural stability of firearm markets, our findings clarify why cross-sectional studies may overstate associations between firearm prevalence and social outcomes, while panel approaches that absorb fixed differences more accurately capture within-area dynamics. The results have implications for evaluating policies that aim to modify local firearm environments, and for interpreting empirical evidence on guns, crime, and public safety.

title: Strategic Grid Modernization for Enhanced Energy Security and Industrial Competitiveness: A Multi-Pillar Framework for the United States

detail.title: Strategic Grid Modernization for Enhanced Energy Security and Industrial Competitiveness: A Multi-Pillar Framework for the United States
detail.abstract: The United States electrical grid faces unprecedented challenges from surging demand, cybersecurity threats, and climate-related disruptions. This paper presents a comprehensive strategic framework for grid modernization organized around three interdependent pillars: technological innovation and deployment, regulatory reform and workforce development, and strategic public-private partnerships. Drawing on comparative analysis of international approaches and synthesizing current policy gaps, we propose actionable recommendations including accelerated smart grid deployment, streamlined transmission permitting, mandatory cybersecurity standards, and domestic supply chain fortification. Our phased implementation strategy projects that achieving 80% renewable integration, 99.97% grid reliability, and elimination of foreign dependency for critical components is feasible within a ten-year horizon given appropriate policy support and investment frameworks. The framework positions grid modernization not merely as infrastructure renewal but as a strategic imperative for maintaining American industrial competitiveness and national security in the 21st century.

title: Business Variety Scale (BVS): An Organic Framework for Measuring Organizational Variety

detail.title: Business Variety Scale (BVS): An Organic Framework for Measuring Organizational Variety
detail.abstract: This working paper introduces the Business Variety Scale (BVS), an empirically-validated framework for measuring organizational complexity across 12 dimensions. Analyzing 471 Fortune 500 companies (94.2% coverage) using objective XBRL financial data from SEC filings, we reveal that industry characteristics-not company size-primarily determine organizational complexity patterns. Energy & Utilities companies average 4.73 BVS (highest complexity) while Technology companies average 3.59 BVS (focused complexity). The research uncovers a counterintuitive variety-performance paradox: high-variety companies achieve superior Fortune 500 rankings (average rank 245.2 vs 262.3) despite lower operational efficiency ($1,291K vs $1,669K revenue per employee), suggesting successful firms deliberately accept efficiency tradeoffs for strategic positioning advantages. The framework enables executives to benchmark complexity against industry-specific norms across 13 industry categories and 66 specific classifications, identify dimensions driving competitive advantage, and plan strategic variety expansion within sustainable limits. Complete with weighted calculation methodology, opensource Python implementation, comprehensive industry benchmarks, dimensional analysis, and company-level relative positioning data. All code and datasets available at www.galaxiez.com.

title: Residential Perceptions of Neighborhood Livability, Satisfaction, and Loyalty in Central City Neighborhoods. Case Study: Shahrood, Iran

detail.title: Residential Perceptions of Neighborhood Livability, Satisfaction, and Loyalty in Central City Neighborhoods. Case Study: Shahrood, Iran
detail.abstract: Neighborhoods surrounding historical markets in Iranian cities have experienced a decline in residential interest in recent years, with many long-time residents migrating to other areas. Despite the abundance of infrastructure and facilities in these areas, the decline in residential quality will cause irreparable damage to the urban economy and the social fabric of city centers. The research hypothesis is that the decline in the quality of livability in these neighborhoods has led to a decrease in the level of satisfaction with housing and loyalty to the neighborhoods, resulting in a reduction of the desire to live in these areas. The authors conducted this research through irregular cluster sampling in the neighborhoods surrounding the historic market of Shahrood using 385 researcher-made questionnaires. The findings showed that, despite some performance shortcomings, residents' willingness to stay or recommend the location to others remains high. This positive willingness among residents could be due to emotional factors, social capital, or a sense of place attachment. Improving performance in environmental dimensions has a direct role in increasing resident satisfaction. It also has an impact on loyalty. Satisfaction plays a crucial role in transferring the positive effects of environmental quality to a sense of loyalty towards one's place of residence. The subjective perception of the importance of environmental components can ultimately strengthen loyalty to the place by mediating performance and satisfaction. The study's results provide urban design strategies to enhance the livability of the aforementioned areas by prioritizing them according to the quadrants of the importance-performance matrix.

title: Antitrust Analysis of Search Engine Defaults
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School and Stanford Law School

detail.title: Antitrust Analysis of Search Engine Defaults
detail.abstract:
In a search engine default agreement, a search engine pays to be the default search option on another firm’s browser or other search-related product. These agreements, which are at the heart of the Google Search monopolization case, raise challenging and important questions for antitrust policy. This article provides a comprehensive analysis of these antitrust issues. We first explore the economic effects of search defaults, examining possible pro- and anticompetitive effects on both static (short-run) and dynamic (long-run) competition. Second, we explore important legal issues raised by the case, including its implications for judicial analysis of harm to competition and causation under Section 2 of the Sherman Act and a number of issues relating to affirmative defenses. Finally, we discuss remedies, applying general principles to a wide range of possible behavioral and structural remedies.

Although defaults create relatively small switching costs, their impact on competition is magnified by data-driven scale effects that lead a search algorithm’s quality to rise and fall with its user count. Although Google’s quality surpasses that of all rivals, evidence suggests that its broad default coverage is driven not merely by high quality, but by vastly outbidding rivals for default placements. Based on the record and recent economic research, both empirical and theoretical, we conclude that very broad defaults by a dominant firm are likely to be harmful overall, particularly to dynamic competition. By contrast, when used in moderation, defaults perform important procompetitive functions, such as fostering entry and investment. If, as in the Google Search case, a court finds serious anticompetitive effects but cannot discern the extent to which they contributed to the defendant’s dominance, this should not necessarily preclude liability. It should, however, limit the scope of appropriate remedies.

title: What Kinds of Behaviour are Engendered by the Hope of Profit?

detail.title: What Kinds of Behaviour are Engendered by the Hope of Profit?
detail.abstract:
From the fluorescent boardrooms of Fortune 500s to the emerging startups sprouting in garages, the hope of profit fuels modern enterprise. It encourages employees to overwork, drives entrepreneurs to risk everything, and convinces parents to invest in their children’s education in hopes of a promising future. But this relentless pursuit of gain also breeds a darker ecosystem where selfishness often outpaces service, and ethics bend to quarterly goals.

What behaviours emerge under this paradigm? And is it superior to what we might observe if all enterprises were governed by public or charitable motives?

This essay argues that while the hope of profit often inspires productivity, innovation, economic growth, and maximizes efficiency and responds quickly to consumer demand; it also encourages self-interest, short-termism, and moral ambiguity. In contrast, enterprises owned by charities or governments may promote social well-being but risk inefficiency, entitlement, and mission drift. Conclusively, neither structure is inherently better; and thus, this essay contends that the most socially optimal behaviours emerge not from one extreme or the other, but from hybrid models that balance profit with purpose.

detail.abstract: The Internal Multi-Ailerons System (IMAS) is an advanced AI-driven aerodynamic control architecture designed to enhance UAV stability, precision, and stealth in extreme flight conditions. The system employs multiple internal ailerons operated autonomously through a hybrid Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework, ensuring real-time balance and adaptability during turbulence, low-speed manoeuvres, and missile deployment. IMAS integrates an intelligent sensor fusion network-combining IMU, GNSS/RTK, air data, and pressure feedback-to maintain optimal positioning and responsiveness. Additionally, it incorporates LED camouflage and radar-absorbent materials for low observability and anti-radar protection. This integration of intelligent control, aerodynamic optimization, and stealth technology establishes IMAS as a foundational innovation for the seventh generation of UAV bombardiers, enabling precise mission performance with superior aerodynamic resilience and survivability.

detail.abstract: This case study examines hierarchy culture as defined within the Competing Values Framework, emphasizing the values of stability, order, and control as the foundation of organizational effectiveness. Through the story of Atlas Industries-a Japanese-founded global manufacturing company-it illustrates how hierarchy enables consistency, reliability, and accountability in complex, high-risk environments. The narrative traces the evolution from founder Kenji Tanaka's rigid, rule-based leadership to successor Naomi Hayes's adaptive transformation program, "Project Equilibrium," which sought to preserve hierarchy's virtues while infusing flexibility and trust. The study explores hierarchy's historical roots in classical management theory, its strengths in ensuring procedural discipline and its vulnerabilities in the face of rapid technological and market change. Ultimately, it argues that hierarchy's enduring relevance lies not in resisting change but in managing it responsibly: sustaining discipline as a platform for learning and adaptability in the digital age. The transformation of Atlas illustrates that order and agility are not opposing forces but complementary imperatives for organizational resilience.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an alternative estimation approach for functional-coefficient panel-data models with sample-selection and fixed-effects that relaxes the identification-condition currently used in the literature. We propose a pairwise-differencing strategy that avoids the zero-sum restriction on the fixed-effects while maintaining the same rate of convergence. We establish the estimator's asymptotic properties and show through simulations that it outperforms existing methods even when their identification condition is satisfied, while also delivering superior computational efficiency by eliminating the need to estimate individual fixed effects.

detail.abstract:
This paper is the national report for Latvia in the project "Mapping Judicial Review of Competition Law Decisions", directed by Or Brook and Barry Rodger. The project is based on an empirical exercise with all decisions taken in judicial review of competition law cases between 2004 and 2020 (excluding merger cases and private enforcement). 

This chapter addressed the judicial review of public enforcement of competition law in Latvia. Overall, the Latvian courts are competent to review all substantive and procedural aspects of the Competition Council's decisions. The courts are also competent to review (but not to substitute with their own assessment) those elements of any decision related to the setting of a fine. The courts are not limited to facts, evidence and the assessment presented by the Competition Council in its decisions, but when additional assessments are made, they should strictly serve to ascertain that, even regardless of any new considerations, the authority’s decision remains. The Latvian legal framework’s approach to reviewing Competition Council decisions strikes a delicate balance between rigorous judicial scrutiny and the autonomous roles of the judiciary and executive branches.

The low annulment rate of Competition Council decisions, as evidenced by the specific cases cited, reflects a tendency towards strong judicial restraint in overturning administrative decisions. This restraint is further manifested in the nuanced approach of the courts to different types of appeal grounds, with a slightly higher, but highly fluctuating over the years, success rate for substantive appeals.

detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effects of macroprudential policies on the entire distribution of GDP growth for advanced European economies using a narrative-identification strategy in a quantile-regression framework. While macroprudential policy has near-zero effects on the centre of the GDP-growth distribution, tighter policy brings benefits by reducing the variance of future growth, significantly boosting the left tail while simultaneously reducing the right. Assessing a range of channels through which these effects materialise, we find that macroprudential policy particularly operates through ‘credit-at-risk’: it reduces the right tail of future credit growth, dampening booms, in turn reducing the likelihood of extreme GDP-growth outturns.

detail.title: Tax-Motivated Firm Splitting

detail.abstract: How do corporate tax systems shape the boundaries of the firm? This paper shows that nonlinear corporate income taxation can distort firms' organizational structures by inducing tax-motivated firm splitting. I use administrative data on corporations and their owners and exploit two reforms that altered the tax benefits and costs of dividing a firm into multiple entities. First, I show that a temporary increase in the tax advantage of splitting reduces the share of firms filing jointly for corporate income tax purposes. Second, once the benefit is perceived as permanent and minimum capital requirements for new firms are abolished, the number of firms per entrepreneur rises significantly and persistently. Finally, I show that reorganizations are primarily driven by tax motives, as I find no effect on firms' total assets, employment, or industry diversification. These findings highlight extensive-margin responses of business organization to corporate taxation, with relevant implications for the understanding of firm dynamics and for tax design.

detail.abstract: This paper examines income and employment outcomes for immigrants in Sweden's most immigrant-dense neighbourhoods between 1998 and 2022. While relative employment among immigrants has improved, relative incomes in these neighbourhoods have stagnated or declined. The most plausible explanation for the persisting income gap and the shrinking employment gap between immigrant-dense and other neighbourhoods is that immigrants in immigrant-dense neighbourhoods are increasingly channelled into non-standard employment. If we look at all immigrants, regardless of where they live, gaps between immigrants and natives are shrinking, both in terms of income and employment. Reconciling these patterns, we show that individuals in immigrant-dense neighbourhoods who enter employment are more likely to relocate to other areas.

detail.abstract: Nigeria’s 2025 tax reform package comprising the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 (NTA), the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 (NTAA), Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act, 2025 (NRSA) and the Joint Revenue Board of Nigeria (Establishment) Act, 2025 (JREA) symbolizes a systemic attempt to simplify the country’s fragmented tax architecture, harmonize administration across tiers of government, and pivot the regime for a digitalizing economy. This article critically assesses the reforms against the chronic problems of multiplicity of taxes, weak coordination, and compliance-frictions for Small Medium Enterprise, and limited coverage of the digital economy. It analyses key innovations consolidation of core tax rules into a single NTA, fiscalization and e-invoicing, new taxpayer rights and administrative rules, the creation of a centralized revenue service, and a national joint revenue governance framework with an Ombudsman and an expanded Tax Appeal Tribunal (TAT). It argues that while the package coheres with long-standing expert recommendations and global trends (e.g., Base Erosion and Profit Shifting 2.0, e-invoicing), success turns on transitional clarity, intergovernmental buy-in, and Micro Small and Medium Enterprise-friendly implementation. The article concludes with practical recommendations to lock in simplification gains without over-burdening the real economy.

detail.title: Interpretable Factors of Firm Characteristics
detail.abstract: We develop a new framework for constructing factors from firm characteristics that balances statistical efficiency and economic interpretability. Instead of using all characteristics equally, our method groups related characteristics and extracts one factor per group. Applied to the IPCA model by Kelly, Pruitt and Su (2019), this approach produces economically meaningful factors that match or exceed standard IPCA in pricing performance. Empirically, we show our parsimonious and transparent factors offer new insights into the drivers of stock returns and outperform existing benchmarks in out-of-sample tests, demonstrating the value of embedding economic structure into statistical modeling. Our framework reveals a clean separation between risk-based factors and those capturing persistent mispricing, offering a sharper lens into the economic channels behind return predictability.

detail.abstract:
The landscape of higher education financing has undergone dramatic transformation over the past three decades, marked by escalating costs, increased reliance on student loans, and evolving repayment dynamics. Against this backdrop, the TIAA Institute, in collaboration with Trellis Strategies, embarked on a study to illuminate the complex relationship between student loan borrowers and their debt, particularly in the wake of the unprecedented federal loan repayment pause of 2020–2023. 

Our research sought to answer several crucial questions: How do borrowers make decisions about taking on student loan debt? What drives their choices regarding loan utilization? How did the payment pause impact borrowers' financial behaviors and wellbeing? And perhaps most importantly, how do these patterns vary across different demographic groups? Through a carefully designed survey of 2,001 student loan borrowers, we gained valuable insights into these pressing questions. 

The findings reveal nuanced patterns in borrowing behaviors and loan utilization across demographic groups. The study also uncovered important correlations between budgeting behaviors and loan repayment expectations, with those who maintained budgets displaying greater confidence in their ability to repay their loans.

detail.title: Automatic Enrollment in Public Supplemental Retirement Plans

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the prevalence of automatic enrollment provisions in public sector supplemental retirement plans. Available evidence indicates that relatively few government retirement systems have adopted automatic enrollment provisions for their supplemental retirement saving plans. We explore some factors that might explain this lack of interest in automatic enrollment by public employers, including state laws that specifically prohibit the use of auto enrollment, the overhead costs of adding the policy, the perception that governments are already providing an adequate retirement plan, and union concerns about the impact of reduced take-home pay. 

Virtually all full-time public employees are covered by employer-provided retirement plans. In general, enrollment in these plans is mandatory, i.e., participation is a condition of employment for most full-time workers. In this study, we refer to these plans as the “primary retirement plan” offered by employers. For most career state and local public employees, these pension plans are expected to be their largest source of income in retirement. Historically, almost all these plans were defined benefit (DB) plans, and individuals retiring with 25 to 30 years of service could expect a benefit at retirement equal to, roughly, 50% to 60% of their final earnings. However, over the past two decades, many public sector employers have instituted changes in their DB plans that reduce the value of future retirement benefits. Although most public primary retirement plans remain DB plans, a trend in recent years is for governments to offer defined contribution (DC) or hybrid plans as their primary pension plan.

detail.title: Global Evolution of Research on Neglected and Underutilized Crops in Response to Abiotic Stress: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Visualization
detail.abstract: Neglected and underutilized crops (NUCs) have emerged as strategic alternatives for building climate-resilient, nutrition-sensitive, and sustainable food systems, particularly in regions vulnerable to abiotic stress. This study examines the global evolution of research on NUCs under abiotic stress, highlighting key contributors, thematic priorities, and existing knowledge gaps across five decades. An initial pool of 2,510 peer-reviewed articles was retrieved from Google Scholar, from which 302 Scopus-indexed publications (1972-2024) were selected using PRISMA-based inclusion criteria. Bibliometric analysis was conducted using the bibliometrix R package and VOSviewer to study publication trends, author productivity, institutional contributions, keyword clusters, and collaboration networks. To ensure thematic coherence, studies covering both pathogen-related and abiotic stress responses in NUCs were integrated under a broader resilience and adaptation framework. The trajectory of NUC research unfolds across three developmental stages: (i) early emergence (1972-2006), dominated by localized crop trials and stress screening; (ii) stable expansion (2007-2016), featuring increased crosscountry collaboration; and (iii) rapid diversification (2017-2024), characterized by molecular breeding, drought tolerance, and genomicsdriven strategies. India, South Africa, and the United Kingdom were leading contributors, while Bambara groundnut, climate adaptation, and food security were dominant research themes. This study shows the skewed global attention in NUC research and calls for a strategic rebalancing toward climate-smart, Africa-prioritized crops. It offers a roadmap for equitable research investment, interdisciplinary integration, and alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Spatial and Temporal Boundaries in Difference-in-Differences: A Framework from Navier-Stokes Equation
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: Spatial and Temporal Boundaries in Difference-in-Differences: A Framework from Navier-Stokes Equation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for identifying spatial and temporal boundaries of treatment effects in difference-in-differences designs. Starting from fundamental fluid dynamics equations (Navier-Stokes), we derive conditions under which treatment effects decay exponentially in space and time, enabling researchers to calculate explicit boundaries beyond which effects become undetectable. The framework encompasses both linear (pure diffusion) and nonlinear (advection-diffusion with chemical reactions) regimes, with testable scope conditions based on dimensionless numbers from physics (P\'eclet and Reynolds numbers). We demonstrate the framework's diagnostic capability using air pollution from coal-fired power plants. Analyzing 791 ground-based PM$_{2.5}$ monitors and 189,564 satellite-based NO$_2$ grid cells in the Western United States over 2019-2021, we find striking regional heterogeneity: within 100 km of coal plants, both pollutants show positive spatial decay (PM$_{2.5}$: $\kappa_s = 0.00200$, $d^* = 1,153$ km; NO$_2$: $\kappa_s = 0.00112$, $d^* = 2,062$ km), validating the framework. Beyond 100 km, negative decay parameters correctly signal that urban sources dominate and diffusion assumptions fail. Ground-level PM$_{2.5}$ decays approximately twice as fast as satellite column NO$_2$, consistent with atmospheric transport physics. The framework successfully diagnoses its own validity in four of eight analyzed regions, providing researchers with physics-based tools to assess whether their spatial difference-in-differences setting satisfies diffusion assumptions before applying the estimator. Our results demonstrate that rigorous boundary detection requires both theoretical derivation from first principles and empirical validation of underlying physical assumptions.

title: A Simpler Look At Complexity
affiliations: Monash University , Monash University

detail.title: A Simpler Look At Complexity
detail.abstract: Kelly et al. (2024) use Random Matrix Theory (RMT) to show that highly overparameterized models can deliver superior out-of-sample performance in noisy financial data, challenging classical parsimony. I provide a simpler, transparent alternative grounded in statistical learning fundamentals. Analyzing an idealized Random Fourier Features model-a nonlinear approximation to kernel methods-I decompose the "double descent" in prediction error into a monotonically decreasing approximation bias (the "virtue" of complexity) and a non-monotonic estimation variance (its "cost"). This bias-variance lens not only demystifies the phenomenon but offers a modular framework for finance-specific enhancements, such as theoryguided structured features or adaptive regularization in return prediction. My approach bridges machine learning and asset pricing, enabling clearer diagnostics and practical extensions beyond the opaque RMT paradigm.

detail.title: Simulating Spatial Flows of Urban Carbon Sequestration Services under Supply–Demand Imbalance: A Case Study of China’s Urban Agglomerations

keywords: supply and demand of carbon sequestration services

detail.abstract: Urban agglomerations, as population and economic hubs, play a pivotal role in shaping the balance between carbon sequestration services (CSS) supply and demand, which is essential for achieving China’s dual carbon goals. This study quantified CSS supply in 19 national urban agglomerations for 2000, 2010, and 2020 using the CASA model, and assessed demand based on population density and per capita carbon emissions. A supply–demand index and bivariate LISA were applied to reveal spatial mismatches, while ecological resistance surfaces and circuit theory modeling were used to simulate CSS flows and identify key corridors and bottlenecks. Results show a persistent “high west–low east” supply pattern, with capacity improvements in central–western agglomerations and constraints in rapidly urbanizing eastern regions. Demand hotspots emerged in the Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta, and Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei, widening the east–west imbalance. CSS flows formed networks with western regions showing higher connectivity, while eastern regions were fragmented. Cross-agglomeration corridors present opportunities for integrated carbon governance. These findings demonstrate the potential of circuit theory for modeling ecosystem service flows in polycentric urban systems and provide actionable insights for regional planning, ecological compensation, and coordinated carbon management.

title: Crowding-Out Effects of a Universal Primary Care Policy: Evidence from Brazil

detail.title: Crowding-Out Effects of a Universal Primary Care Policy: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper studies how expanding free primary healthcare affects private insurance coverage, reducing out-of-pocket spending. We exploit the rollout of Brazil’s Family Health Program (PSF), a large-scale community-based intervention that drastically increased the reach of the public health system across municipalities. Using a difference-in-differences strategy, we find that the program led to a 32% decrease in private plan coverage, without affecting formal labor markets, indicating crowd-out effects. The program increased beneficiary-initiated cancellations of private planes. Finally, health outcomes improved where crowd-out was most intense, indicating health gains. We estimate that this crowd-out effect represented savings of USD 34 million to the health system. The results highlight that, in universal systems, expanding public primary care can enhance welfare while reducing reliance on costlier private provision.

detail.title: Who Speaks when the Future is Uncertain? The Role of Ownership
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how ownership structure and identity shape voluntary disclosure in uncertain times. Using a sample of 11,254 annual earnings announcements by 1,369 European firms during 2015-2022 and the COVID pandemic as a quasi-natural experiment, we find that firms with concentrated ownership respond to increased uncertainty by making longer but more cautious disclosures, while widely held firms show the opposite reaction. Among concentrated owners, founding families exhibit the weakest reaction, followed by non-founding families, and then by other controlling shareholders. These findings confirm that ownership concentration and identity are important sources of systematic variation across firms in their disclosure behavior in response to increased uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Takeaways • Migratory flows are shaped by factors linked to the origin countries (push factors), but also by factors specific to the destination countries (pull factors). This is particularly the case in Spain, where the latter have historically been highly significant. They have also become increasingly important in recent years for explaining migrant flows to Spain and other advanced economies. • Among the specific factors in destination countries that can drive the arrival of migrants are: (i) a reduction in the unemployment rate, (ii) higher average wages and (iii) changes in migration policies that make it easier for migrants and their families to obtain stable residence status. • The economic and social conditions of the countries of origin also significantly influence migratory flows, as shown by the "push" effect generated by political instability, conflicts, natural disasters and food crises, alongside low GDP per capita.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether higher ownership stakes by portfolio managers and senior executives attract fund flows and whether such ownership predicts future performance. Using a sample of 1,436 Chinese equity-oriented mutual funds from 2012 to 2023, we find that higher managerial and senior ownership are significantly associated with larger inflows, suggesting that investors may view ownership as a positive signal of fund quality. However, we find no evidence that ownership forecasts superior performance. Our results indicate that while ownership can embody both incentive-alignment and promotional motives, the marketing channel dominates under the current incentive environment. In this sense, ownership disclosure functions predominantly as a persuasive device that shapes investor perception more than it reveals managerial ability, thereby weakening the link between capital flows and true skill in the mutual fund industry.

detail.abstract: This paper explores how different margins of market share are related to firm markups and their implications for misallocation. Using merged microdata on producers and consumers, we document that while firms’ market shares are related mainly to their number of customers, their price-cost markups are associated only with their average sales per customer. We develop a new model with endogenous customer acquisition that reflects this empirical evidence. When calibrated, this model predicts a higher degree of markup dispersion, which suggests greater efficiency losses due to customer misallocation. An analysis of the efficient allocation in this model reveals that compared with the equilibrium, aggregate TFP and output are 12.2% and 25.5% higher, respectively.

publicationDetails.detailsText: African Journal of Science, Technology, Innovation and Development, 0[10.1080/20421338.2025.2543276]

detail.abstract: This study investigates the antecedents of purchase intentions on TikTok Shop, utilizing Uses and Gratification (U&G) Theory to analyze the impact of entertainment, informativeness, cost savings and attractiveness on student purchase intentions. The study gathered responses from 357 students through an online survey and analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. The results indicate that entertainment, comprehensive informative content and visual appeal significantly influence purchase intention, while cost savings show negligible influence. These results highlight the principal role of engaging and informative content over financial incentives in shaping purchase intention within the digital marketplace environment. This study contributes to the digital marketing literature by contextualizing Uses and Gratification Theory within TikTok Shop, offering a comprehensive understanding of how gratification factors influence this specific demographic group on emerging digital platforms. However, the limitations of the study, given its single institution focus, and lack of generalization, warrant further research. Therefore, future studies should expand the coverage and consider moderating variables such as product type, age, income level and shopping goals.

detail.abstract: We examine how physician and patient behavior shape prescribing patterns by exploiting policy variation from medical marijuana legalization (MML) and recreational marijuana legalization (RML). MML requires a physician visit to obtain a card, engaging a doctor-learning channel, whereas RML permits access without medical oversight, reflecting a patient-behavior channel. Using a difference-indifferences design with Medicare Part D claims from 2014-2019, we find that MML leads to sizable reductions in prescription volumes across most therapeutic classes, while RML generates smaller or offsetting effects. Consistent with the proposed mechanisms, the number of Medicare Part D beneficiaries increases after MML but not after RML, indicating more physician encounters under MML. We further find no evidence of adverse welfare impacts, as in-hospital mortality and inpatient charges remain unaffected by MML. Heterogeneity analyses show that physician competition, physician gender, and urban-rural status meaningfully shape these effects, highlighting the importance of local provider and patient contexts in mediating policy outcomes.

detail.title: Old Wine in New bottles: Rare Earth Elements and the New Extractivism Path of Kazakhstan
detail.abstract: The rising global demand for Rare Earth Elements (REEs) and uranium-driven by the imperatives of decarbonization and strategic autonomy-has repositioned resource-rich countries at the centre of the energy transition debate. Kazakhstan, historically dependent on oil and extractive exports, is now emerging as a key player in the REE and uranium markets. This paper interrogates whether this pivot represents a genuine structural transformation or a continuity of extractivist dependency under the guise of green development. By analysing Kazakhstan's evolving role in global REE supply chains, its uranium export structure, the balance-of-payment implications, and the ownership dynamics of its critical minerals sectors, our work examines the tension between geopolitical opportunity and financial subordination. We argue that without strategic industrial policy, sovereign investment frameworks, and a reconfiguration of the country's insertion into global value chains, Kazakhstan risks replicating the same patterns of enclave production and macroeconomic vulnerability that have historically characterized its oil-based development model.

detail.title: The Age of Engineered Belief: Why Human Psychology Still Outperforms AI Marketing

keywords: the 23 laws of marketing master them or die

detail.abstract: Human beings built machines to study desire, then forgot that desire still owns the machines. This commentary examines how algorithmic marketing, though mathematically precise, remains subordinate to the ancient circuitry of human psychology. The illusion of autonomy, emotional contagion, and cognitive bias continue to dictate what converts and what collapses, no matter how advanced the model. Building on The 23 Laws of Marketing and the Machiavellian Marketing Framework, this piece argues that true influence is not achieved through data volume but through narrative control: the ability to shape what people feel before they think. AI may automate persuasion, but only psychology engineers belief.
